Cape Town Taxi Strike 2023

By: Marion Edmunds | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We look at the stand-off between the authorities and the taxi industry and why the best intentions were unable to stop a strike which has resulted in death and destruction in the city

Unique Selling Point:
We follow up a week of dramatic breaking news to give an in-depth analysis of the intractable problems preventing a resolution to the stand off between taxi bosses, their soldiers on the ground, and the city and provincial authorities. Behind the chaos, are patterns of behaviour on both sides which have re-inforced the contest for control of the roads.

Summary:
It’s been a week of reckoning in the long running contest between the city and the provincial authorities on the one hand and the taxi industry on the other as to who owns Cape Town’s roads. On Thursday afternoon, the taxis suspended their services in a stay-away set until Thursday the 10th of August. Commuters were left stranded, some having to walk as far as 50s kilometres to their homes on dangerous roads – and some never made it. And the violence – bus burning, looting and attacks – began almost immediately as anonymous trouble-makers sowed chaos on commuter transport routes.

In the run up to the stand-off, the city and province authorities were due to meet SANTACO, the South African National Taxi Council, on Monday to discuss the controversial campaign of impoundments spearheaded by Cape Town’s MEC for Safety and Security, JP Smith. Observing that fines were not improving either the driving of taxis, nor their respect for the rule of law, Smith has shifted the penalty for disobeying rules from fines to impounding of the taxis. Since new bylaws were enacted, the impoundments have picked up in number, causing increasing inconvenience to taxi bosses, and more money out of their pocket. For them, JP Smith has become the face of kragdadigheid, and in texts circulated they name him personally as the problem.

“He is consumed with his own sense of power and privilege and a deep-seated hatred for the taxi industry, which he often brands as thugs, mafia, criminals etc. He does not care about the fate of the poor. The ability for the poor to fend for themselves is facilitated through the taxis taking them to work-places. His constant unfair impoundments put many livelihoods at risk,” said SANTACO on Wednesday third of August, reacting to videos of a stand-off between law enforcement and taxis on the roof of the old station in Cape Town, a location notorious for crime and muggings. The tussle, which saw law enforcement officers break open windows, sparked a change of tactics on behalf of SANTACO.

The stand-off between JP Smith and the taxi industry is only one element in this toxic story. The taxi industry pulled out of the Industry Task Team group altogether, abandoning the platform on which they could discuss their grievances. They then held a meeting in Khayelitsha and invited all transport providers – including bus and e-hailing drivers – as well as all political parties except for the DA. The meeting had the air of a political rally and was addressed by former discredited ANC leader Marius Fransman. The EFF toyi-toyied, and the meeting drew everybody into the stay-away, supported by the opposition parties. Minister of Police Bheki Cele was at the venue before the meeting, and interacted with the taxi bosses.

On their list of grievances is operating licences for certain routes, which the industry argues need to be serviced following the collapse of the rail system. They are also unhappy generally about the way the law is enforced on the roads.

A source told me that members of that meeting on leaving the hall immediately pelted a My Citi-bus with stones and the driver only just managed to get away. At the same time SANTACO has attempted to distance itself from the violence by sending out press statements saying that it distanced itself from the violence.

In desperation Golden Arrow, the only bus system trying to operate, has got a court order against all the taxi associations not to attack the buses. But six buses had been burnt by Monday morning and the bus service is calling for security back-up.

Attempts to mediate continued during the weekend but collapsed, allegedly because law enforcement tried to frisk the taxi bosses security detail. (This is unconfirmed). So Monday started with burning busses, blockades, missing commuters and at least one murder. The airport is difficult to access and people are finding it very difficult to come to work safely.

On Friday, things were no better. Buses were torched and commuters harassed, hospitals closed and people unable to go to work or school.

The strike is meant to culminate on Women’s Day when President Cyril Ramaphosa will address a national commemorative event at the Khayelitsha Rugby stadium. The industry plans to protest at the venue and ask for the President to hear their grievances. In the meantime, the city, the province and commuters are running out of patience, laying the scene for an ongoing showdown, most likely with tragic consequences for people outside of the dispute.

Press Release:


Cape Town’s Taxi Stand-off
It’s been a week of reckoning in the city of Cape Town as the long running contest between the authorities and the taxi industry came to a head. On Thursday last week, taxi bosses unexpectedly suspended their services in the afternoon, to embark on a week-long stay-away that left thousands of desperate commuters stranded. On dangerous roads and highways, some people including school children began the long walk home into the night, to far-flung townships on the outskirts of the city. The violence started immediately – burning buses, looting and sporadic attacks – as troublemakers sowed chaos on commuter transport routes and intimidated workers trying to get to work. But the stand-off continued as the taxi industry demanded that the city stop impounding their vehicles for breaking the law. The city and provincial authorities on the other hand, remained resolute, turning to the courts to bolster their defences. But it’s now a political minefield, as national government steps in to muddy the waters, and divisions harden at the negotiating table and among angry communities on the ground.
Producer: Marion Edmunds | Presenter: Erin Bates

VO SCRIPT
CAPE TOWN TAXI STRIKE #6420

(VO) IT STARTED LIKE ANY OTHER WINTER MORNING…
BUT BY THE AFTERNOON, EVERYTHING HAD CHANGED…
A SHOW OF FORCE FROM THE TAXI INDUSTRY LOCKED THE CITY DOWN -
WITH WORSE TO COME.

Strike Launch Piece To Camera
On Thursday the third of August Cape Town taxi bosses called a meeting with private transport providers and opposition political parties. And from there they launched a stay-away with immediate effect.

(VO) MANDLA HERMANUS, THE CHAIRPERSON OF THE SOUTH AFRICAN NATIONAL TAXI COUNCIL, CALLED FOR A TRANSPORT STRIKE.
Mandla Hermanus talking in the hall:
2:13 All of us to say, we have now to say enough is enough….

(VO) WITHIN MINUTES OF THE MEETING ENDING, BUSES WERE TARGETS.
THEN PRIVATE CARS AND PEOPLE TOO.
IN A CAMPAIGN OF URBAN TERROR.

Charly’s Bakery Piece to Cam
Despite the turmoil one city bakery was determined to keep the oven on and tweeted updates on what staff endured as they tried to get to and from work.

(VO) JACQUI BIESS EMPLOYS TWENTY PEOPLE TO MAKE FANTASTICAL CAKES FOR CAPE TOWN.
IN THE CHAOS OF THE STRIKE, HER BAKER, PENELOPE MTHIYANE COULD NOT FIND HER GRANDSON.

JACQUI BIESS
OWNER: CHARLY’S BAKERY
2:12 Her grandson of 11 years old was still missing. So she didn't want to leave. She didn't want to get out of contact and we were panicking on her behalf. Finally, she got home at nine o'clock. And she said but Qwaqambile is not home yet. … this is when I got into Twitter and I said I need help.

PENELOPE MTHIYANE
BAKER: CHARLY’S BAKERY
UPSOUND FROM PENELOPE ZOOM : 1:44 I was looking up and down, the people they were standing on the queue, b money to, but I didn't manage to stand on the queue because of him. I was looking up and down, looking up and down, looking for him…5:43 I was crying at the same time, but that you didn't know. I didn't want people to see. I was crying
Oh where I'm going next. I just wipe for the people not to see me, I am crying.

(VO) THE TRAUMATISED CHILD HITCH-HIKED AND WALKED HOME, ARRIVING TWO HOURS BEFORE MIDNIGHT.

JACQUI BIESS
OWNER: CHARLY’S BAKERY
3:47 it's just not on this is it's not on, the taxis do this to our children and our old people and my staff, the few people who are earning a living in our country who are employed and they are forced to walk along the highway to get home. This is not right. This is evil.

(VO) SOME OF THE BAKERY EMPLOYEES LIVE IN KAYAMANDI, NEAR STELLENBOSCH. HERE AS IN MANY OTHER HOTSPOTS, CRIMINAL ELEMENTS LOOTED AND BURNT.

(VO) BUT A RESOLUTE CORDON OF ARMED OFFICERS HELD THE LINE….

(VO) DAY IN….

(VO) AND DAY OUT….


(VO) THE MINISTER OF POLICE WAS ON THE SCENE.
BHEKI CELE
MINISTER: SAFETY AND SECURITY
A total of five murders were recorded to during the period in question.

SKY NEWS READER:We have some breaking news now…

(VO) ONE OF THE VICTIMS WAS A BRITISH SURGEON.
HE WAS MURDERED IN HIS CAR IN NYANGA IN FRONT OF HIS WIFE AND TODDLER.
SKY NEWS READER:.It is believed that the took the wrong turn from the nearby airport, a group then approached the vehicle and then shot him

(VO) A LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICER WAS SHOT DEAD ON THE SAME DAY, LEAVING BEHIND A FAMILY OF FOUR.
A TAXI DRIVER WAS AMONG THE FATALITIES.

BHEKI CELE
MINISTER: SAFETY AND SECURITY
08:58 … 120 people have been arrested. ….09: 53 it's important that while the law enforcement is taking place, people must be negotiating.

(VO) THE LOCAL TAXI INDUSTRY HAD PLACED DEMANDS ON THE TABLE.
THEY WANT MORE PERMITS, THEY WANT STATE SUBSIDIES, AND EXCLUSIVE HIGH SPEED LANES
BUT MOST OF ALL THEY WANT TO HALT WHAT THEY SAY IS AN UNFAIR CAMPAIGN TO IMPOUND TAXIS FOR BREAKING THE LAW.

MANDLA HERMANUS
SANTACO: CHAIRPERSON
5:31…. as long as our vehicles are impounded at this rate, we have to continue to show that we are not happy

(VO) PREVIOUS PROTESTS HAD LED TO THE SETTING UP OF A SPECIAL TASK FORCE FOR NEGOTIATIONS.
BUT THREE DAYS BEFORE THE STRIKE, DETENTE HAD BROKEN DOWN.

Station Deck Video Piece to Cam
It was here at the station deck in the city centre that a law enforcement operation turned ugly. And taxi bosses were so enraged by dramatic footage of the incident that they walked out of talks with local government leaders.

(VO) THIS VIDEO WENT VIRAL.
THE TAXI INDUSTRY BLAMED LAW ENFORCEMENT IN GENERAL BUT CAPE TOWN’S CONTROVERSIAL MAYORAL COMMITTEE MEMBER, JP SMITH, IN PARTICULAR.

(VO) BUT SMITH INSISTS THE CLIP WAS TAKEN OUT OF CONTEXT, AS PEOPLE INSIDE THE TAXI HAD FIRST SHOT AT OFFICERS FROM BEHIND TINTED WINDOWS.

J.P. SMITH
SAFETY AND SECURITY: CITY OF CAPE TOWN
5:37 the lawful instruction was given to the occupants to exit the vehicle. …The occupants declined, a lawful instruction then again was given to breach the vehicle.

(VO) SMITH IS THE FACE OF THE CRACKDOWN, PUSHING IMPOUNDMENTS AND TIGHTENING UP LOOPHOLES WITH NEW BYLAWS.

J.P. SMITH
SAFETY AND SECURITY: CITY OF CAPE TOWN
09:30 the enforcement's done in terms of a national act, not a city by law. …. And in the case of Cape Town, they may be they the argument may be well we enforce it too diligently. I don't believe that's true. ……we get 1000s of complaints a week about Taxis 1000s Literally, it's the top complaints category to the city.

(VO) MID-WEEK SMITH VISITED THE GOLDEN ARROW BUS COMPANY TO SURVEY THE STRIKE DAMAGE.
THE CORNER OF THE EPPING DEPOT IS DUBBED THE GRAVEYARD BY THE COMPANY’S SPOKESPERSON, BRONWEN DYKE-BEYER.

BRONWEN DYKE-BEYER
SPOKESPERSON: GABS
0:14 Within about an hour and a half the buses were set alight in Nyanga terminus, which is traditionally a hotspot for these kinds of taxi strikes and stay aways . And then another two buses were lost. Later on in the day, on Friday, we lost another two buses. And then just lots of incidents of intimidation, one of our bus drivers was shot in the leg during a burning incident. So very, very difficult operating circumstances.

(VO) DURING THE STRIKE, POLICE ESCORTED A SKELETON BUS SERVICE, PROTECTING THOSE COMMUTERS BRAVE ENOUGH TO VENTURE OUT.

(VO) SANTACO SHRUGGED OFF ANY BLAME FOR THE VIOLENCE, WITH STATEMENTS CIRCULATED ON SOCIAL MEDIA.
NCEBE ENGE
FIRST DEPUTY CHAIR: SANTACO
We also want to distance ourselves as SANTACO in the riot that is taking place in our commuters - communities. We are not part of that.

(VO) AMID THE ACCUSATIONS AND DENIALS, THE IMPACT ON COMMUTERS, SCHOOLS AND BUSINESSES WAS DEVASTATING.

(VO) NEGOTIATIONS WERE EASILY THROWN OFF COURSE..
ON SUNDAY NIGHT, SKITTISH TAXI BOSSES UNEXPECTEDLY QUIT TALKS
BECAUSE THEIR SECURITY TEAM WERE CARRYING AUTOMATIC RIFLES AND WERE DENIED ENTRY BY POLICE.

(VO) RICARDO MACKENZIE IS THE PROVINCE’S LEAD NEGOTIATOR. HE STUCK TO HIS GUNS.

RICARDO MACKENZIE
MEC FOR MOBILITY, WESTERN CAPE
06:42 Impoundments as now seem to be the only deterrants to stop unroadworthy vehicles, vehicles operating without a driver's licence,if you drunk on the minibus taxi, your vehicle will also be impounded. And that is one of the big sticking points, that I'm surprised that the leaders of SANTACO …want us to allow a vehicle to continue operating whilst the driver is drunk.

Party politics Piece to Cam
There's taxi politics, and then there's party politics. And inevitably, a year before a national election, a crisis like this becomes an opportunity for grandstanding.

(VO) CASE IN POINT, THE NATIONAL MINISTER FOR TRANSPORT, SINDISWE CHIKUNGA, WHO APPEARED TO SIDE WITH SANTACO, SAYING THAT THE CITY’S IMPOUNDMENTS MAY BE UNLAWFUL.

RICARDO MACKENZIE
MEC FOR MOBILITY, WESTERN CAPE
16:39 The negotiations has been tough. And being the lead negotiator in that room, when my colleague, the Minister of Transport whose legislation that I'm implementing stood up in that meeting, me against thirty men, and sided with them was the most bizarre thing I've ever seen in my life.

(VO) IT WAS STALEMATE BY MID-WEEK,
CONCERNED COMMUNITY LEADERS CALLED A SPECIAL SERVICE AT ST GEORGE’S CATHEDRAL.

LLEWELLYN MACMASTER
MODERATOR: UNITED REFORM CHURCH
6:17 People cannot afford this. I mean, they cannot afford not going to work. Children cannot afford being out of school, What are you going to do about the fact that shelves are empty in townships,

ERIN BATES: People don't have food?
LM: People don't have food.

(VO) THE PRAYERS FOR PEACE WERE ATTENDED BY TAXI LEADERS AND THE MAYOR, GEORDIN HILL-LEWIS.

UPSOUND FROM MAYOR: 0:52 When you deal with a situation like this, you really do need sometimes the wisdom of Solomon to know what is right. And you just have to stand by a few basic principles echoed in our service here today that violence is ungodly.

(VO) ON DAY SEVEN OF THE STRIKE, THE MOOD WAS SOMBRE. THE TAXI INDUSTRY WAS LOSING R50 MILLION A DAY

UPSOUND FROM MANDLA HERMANUS 02:42 we feel the pain of our commuters, we are feeling the pain ourselves, because it's our vehicles, it's us who are not going to be able to meet the monthly repayments at the end of this month.

(VO) ALL PARTIES HAVE NOW TURNED TO THE COURTS FOR CLARITY ON THE LAW AND PROTECTION FROM VIOLENCE. THIS STRATEGY IN PART ALLOWED A RETURN TO NEGOTIATIONS.

Ricardo Mackenzie Tik Tok:
It’s a great relief to see all the taxi’s are getting back to work
(VO) LATE THURSDAY, NEWS BROKE ON SOCIAL MEDIA GROUPS THAT THE STRIKE HAD BEEN SUSPENDED.
AND IN A BITTER IRONY FOR ALL CAPETONIANS, THE TERMS OF THE AGREEMENT BETWEEN SANTACO AND THE CITY WERE ALMOST IDENTICAL TO THOSE TABLED A WEEK EARLIER.

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 14 August 2023 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Press Release: Cape Town’s Taxi Stand-off It’s been a week of reckoning in the city of Cape Town as the long running contest between the authorities and the taxi industry came to a head. On Thursday last week, taxi bosses unexpectedly suspended their services in the afternoon, to embark on a week-long stay-away that left thousands of desperate commuters stranded. On dangerous roads and highways, some people including school children began the long walk home into the night, to far-flung townships on the outskirts of the city. The violence started immediately – burning buses, looting and sporadic attacks – as troublemakers sowed chaos on commuter transport routes and intimidated workers trying to get to work. But the stand-off continued as the taxi industry demanded that the city stop impounding their vehicles for breaking the law. The city and provincial authorities on the other hand, remained resolute, turning to the courts to bolster their defences. But it’s now a political minefield, as national government steps in to muddy the waters, and divisions harden at the negotiating table and among angry communities on the ground. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We look at the stand-off between the authorities and the taxi industry and why the best intentions were unable to stop a strike which has resulted in death and destruction in the city
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We follow up a week of dramatic breaking news to give an in-depth analysis of the intractable problems preventing a resolution to the stand off between taxi bosses, their soldiers on the ground, and the city and provincial authorities. Behind the chaos, are patterns of behaviour on both sides which have re-inforced the contest for control of the roads.
metadata.Summary: It’s been a week of reckoning in the long running contest between the city and the provincial authorities on the one hand and the taxi industry on the other as to who owns Cape Town’s roads. On Thursday afternoon, the taxis suspended their services in a stay-away set until Thursday the 10th of August. Commuters were left stranded, some having to walk as far as 50s kilometres to their homes on dangerous roads – and some never made it. And the violence – bus burning, looting and attacks – began almost immediately as anonymous trouble-makers sowed chaos on commuter transport routes. In the run up to the stand-off, the city and province authorities were due to meet SANTACO, the South African National Taxi Council, on Monday to discuss the controversial campaign of impoundments spearheaded by Cape Town’s MEC for Safety and Security, JP Smith. Observing that fines were not improving either the driving of taxis, nor their respect for the rule of law, Smith has shifted the penalty for disobeying rules from fines to impounding of the taxis. Since new bylaws were enacted, the impoundments have picked up in number, causing increasing inconvenience to taxi bosses, and more money out of their pocket. For them, JP Smith has become the face of kragdadigheid, and in texts circulated they name him personally as the problem. “He is consumed with his own sense of power and privilege and a deep-seated hatred for the taxi industry, which he often brands as thugs, mafia, criminals etc. He does not care about the fate of the poor. The ability for the poor to fend for themselves is facilitated through the taxis taking them to work-places. His constant unfair impoundments put many livelihoods at risk,” said SANTACO on Wednesday third of August, reacting to videos of a stand-off between law enforcement and taxis on the roof of the old station in Cape Town, a location notorious for crime and muggings. The tussle, which saw law enforcement officers break open windows, sparked a change of tactics on behalf of SANTACO. The stand-off between JP Smith and the taxi industry is only one element in this toxic story. The taxi industry pulled out of the Industry Task Team group altogether, abandoning the platform on which they could discuss their grievances. They then held a meeting in Khayelitsha and invited all transport providers – including bus and e-hailing drivers – as well as all political parties except for the DA. The meeting had the air of a political rally and was addressed by former discredited ANC leader Marius Fransman. The EFF toyi-toyied, and the meeting drew everybody into the stay-away, supported by the opposition parties. Minister of Police Bheki Cele was at the venue before the meeting, and interacted with the taxi bosses. On their list of grievances is operating licences for certain routes, which the industry argues need to be serviced following the collapse of the rail system. They are also unhappy generally about the way the law is enforced on the roads. A source told me that members of that meeting on leaving the hall immediately pelted a My Citi-bus with stones and the driver only just managed to get away. At the same time SANTACO has attempted to distance itself from the violence by sending out press statements saying that it distanced itself from the violence. In desperation Golden Arrow, the only bus system trying to operate, has got a court order against all the taxi associations not to attack the buses. But six buses had been burnt by Monday morning and the bus service is calling for security back-up. Attempts to mediate continued during the weekend but collapsed, allegedly because law enforcement tried to frisk the taxi bosses security detail. (This is unconfirmed). So Monday started with burning busses, blockades, missing commuters and at least one murder. The airport is difficult to access and people are finding it very difficult to come to work safely. On Friday, things were no better. Buses were torched and commuters harassed, hospitals closed and people unable to go to work or school. The strike is meant to culminate on Women’s Day when President Cyril Ramaphosa will address a national commemorative event at the Khayelitsha Rugby stadium. The industry plans to protest at the venue and ask for the President to hear their grievances. In the meantime, the city, the province and commuters are running out of patience, laying the scene for an ongoing showdown, most likely with tragic consequences for people outside of the dispute.
